en: Now, at a pure time prior to the performance of the *saṃskāra* rites, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, Nārāyaṇabali, having bathed and purified himself, shall duly worship Viṣṇu and the deceased (preta) as Vaivasvata in a clean place. Standing before them, facing south, with his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnavītin*), he shall offer ten funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) mixed with sesame seeds and soaked in honey and ghee upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, using his left hand. Meditating on the deceased in the form of Viṣṇu, he shall say: "O Kāśyapa-gotra Devadatta, this cake is for you. Having offered the cakes, he shall honor them with perfumes and other offerings and then cast them into the water.

Having performed the *nirvapaṇa* (offering of water), he should cast it into a river. Then, having invited an odd number of Brāhmaṇas during the night and fasted, on the following day at midday, having worshipped Viṣṇu and fed the Brāhmaṇas according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for the sake of the deceased, and when they are satiated, he should silently perform the ritual up to the end of the *ninayana* (pouring of water) near the Brāhmaṇas in the manner of the *piṇḍa* rite. Then, with the remnants of the food, he should offer four *piṇḍas* placed toward the south, saying: "To Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, to Śiva with his retinue, and to Yama; O Viṣṇu, this *piṇḍa* is for you. Thus he should give them. Then...

Having meditated upon the fifth [deity], a preta of the Kāśyapa lineage named Devadatta, one should offer [the oblation] to Viṣṇu in that form, saying, "O Viṣṇu, this is for you. Then, having satisfied those who have sipped water with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should especially gratify one among them who possesses good qualities with garments, ornaments, cattle, gold, and so forth, while maintaining the mental visualization of him as the preta.

Then, having had those who hold sacred grass (pavitra) in their hands offer water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) for the deceased of the Kāśyapa lineage, saying, "This handful of water with sesame seeds is for you," and having caused [the officiant] to recite, "By this Nārāyaṇa-bali rite, may the Blessed Viṣṇu make this Devadatta pure, free from sin, and fit for ritual action," he should dismiss them. This is the procedure for the Nārāyaṇa-bali.

In this same manner, one should worship another deity of one's own choice as a companion to Yama and perform this rite; even such a person becomes free from sin. However, even one who has performed meritorious deeds should not perform rites for the next world without offering this *bali*; if it is not offered, it does not reach [the destination], it perishes in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Therefore, one should perform it according to one's ability. || 15 ||

Now, regarding the *nāgabalih*: having fashioned a five-hooded serpent out of wood or clay for those killed by snakes, one should begin from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of either the month of Bhādrapada or another month, and continue for a year. Every month, on that same day, having fasted, one should bathe the image at night with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and being pure oneself, one should worship it on a clean seat with fragrant scents, flowers, incense, and lamps, and then prostrate.

Every month, having offered an oblation of milk-rice, clarified butter, milk, and cakes to each of the following—ananta, vāsuki, śeṣa, padma, kambala, karkoṭaka, aśvatara, dhṛtarāṣṭra, śaṅkhapāla, kālīya, takṣaka, and kapila—and having kept a vigil, on the following day he should feed the Brāhmaṇas with food containing the three sweets (trivṛt). When the year is complete, having bathed on the fifth lunar day, he should give a golden serpent and a cow to a Brāhmaṇa, feed others as desired, and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

He should cause the *nāgas* to be addressed with words of affection. This is the *nāgabali*. Then, on both sides, on the fifth lunar days (*pañcamī*), having swept the ground clean, he should draw a serpent with flour, worship it with white fragrant scents and other offerings, present milk and sweetmeats, and stand before it, praying, "Release, release Devadatta! He should then eat sweet food together with his kinsmen. Having performed the *Nārāyaṇabali* at the end of the year in the manner described, he should thereafter perform the ritual acts.

Now follows the rite of the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*). On the full moon of Kārttika, Vaiśākha, or Āśvayuja, or under the asterism Revatī, one should select the best son of a cow that has living calves and is rich in milk—a bull from one's own herd that is free from leprosy, not spotted, one or two years old, and either blue, brown, tawny, or red; according to some, it should possess auspicious marks, while others say it may be black, reddish-brown, or white at will. It should be released together with eight heifers, or four.

Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the rite with water containing rice and barley, or with the *āpohiṣṭhīya* verses and the *vāmadevya* chant, and having sprinkled [the person] facing eastward as before, one should kindle a fire on the bank of a river, in a cow-pen, or at a crossroads. Having offered a *sthālīpāka* oblation to Rudra as a complete burnt offering (*sarvahuta*), and having purified [the person] with water from a full vessel using a *saumya* milk-rice dish, a flour-cake, or barley-gruel, one should lead the fire three times around [the person] clockwise and [recite] the four directions with the hymns: *kadrudrāya*, *imā rudrāya*, *ā te pitar*, and *imā rudrāya sthiradhanvane giraḥ*.

Having approached, having released [the calf] facing east or northeast together with a young heifer, [he says]: "I give this youth to you as a drink; sport and roam about with him, your beloved. And you, I join together with offspring, fair speech, abundance of wealth, and nourishment. May the earth be peaceful, may the mid-region be auspicious, and may the divine sky grant us fearlessness."

"May the quarters, the intermediate directions, the upward directions, the waters, and the lightnings protect us on every side"—having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with this verse and the hymn beginning with "The bull among those being measured," whatever he drinks, eats, or tosses his tail filled with water, by that he gratifies the gods, the seers (*ṛṣis*), and the ancestors; he rescues his lineage members seven generations back and seven forward, both preceding and succeeding; and for the sake of the deceased, he delivers him from the great hell. Therefore, on the eleventh day, having given the first monthly offering (*ādyamāsika*), one should release a bull for the deceased; such is this [rite].

The release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) leads to heaven and is beneficial for cattle; it is known from tradition that by releasing a bull, one becomes a great possessor of livestock. Therefore, the Teacher says that one should not fail to release one. Consequently, some perform this rite as a constant obligation and mutter only the *rudra* [mantras], for he alone is the Lord of Creatures (*paśupati*). Having returned home while muttering the *śāntātīya* hymn, and having fed the Brahmins with rice cooked in ghee, one should worship Rudra with the names Agni, Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Śūlin, Bhava, and Mahādeva; or else, one should worship Rudra alone, dedicating the rite as is appropriate, and perform a rite for well-being (*svastyayana*).

One should cause these rites to be recited and perform all of them exactly as stated; thus one attains all auspicious benefits. This is the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*. Homage to Āśvalāyana! Homage to Āśvalāyana! || 18 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the Āśvalāyana-Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa. || 3 ||
